hooks.text: An octopus has three beating hearts and bright blue copper-based blood.
Why do two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live in its arms?
Out of 500 million neurons, an octopus keeps most in its arms.

title: The Animal with Three Hearts and Blue Blood
description: The octopus is a biological marvel with three hearts, blue blood, and a mind distributed throughout its arms.

beats.text: An octopus has three beating hearts and bright blue copper-based blood.
beats.visual: Scientific illustration of a common octopus showing three hearts and circulatory system

beats.text: Stepping up from a single heart, this creature lacks bones entirely and can squeeze through gaps the size of a coin.
beats.visual: Giant Pacific octopus squeezing through a small transparent tube in an aquarium

beats.text: Moving up the ladder of complexity, the entire animal possesses around five hundred million total neurons.
beats.visual: Microscopic view of cephalopod neural tissue or stylized nerve diagram

beats.text: Climbing to the peak of biological weirdness, two-thirds of those cells live directly inside its eight arms.
beats.visual: Close-up of octopus arm showing detailed suckers and nerve paths

beats.text: Because each arm contains more neurons than many small mammals, it can taste, touch, and move without the central brain.
beats.visual: Octopus arm exploring a coral crevice while the head faces another direction

beats.text: This decentralized mind lets veined octopuses walk their arms to collect discarded coconut shells for portable shelter.
beats.visual: Veined octopus carrying coconut shells across the sandy seabed, Indonesia

beats.visual: Common octopus swimming gracefully through clear blue ocean water

better_than_last: Informed by the reviewer, I connected the tool-using behavior in Beat 6 directly to the decentralized neuron count in the arms to provide a stronger payoff for the distributed mind theme.
